bambarakanda-falls.shortDescription: Abseil 650 feet down the face of Sri Lanka's tallest waterfall, set against pine forest and mountain views in Kalupahana.
fullDescription: Bambarakanda Falls is Sri Lanka's tallest waterfall, standing 263 metres (863 ft) in Kalupahana's Badulla District. Reaching the top involves a scenic hike through pine forest before you gear up for a 650-foot abseil down the rock face beside the cascade.

From partway down, the view opens onto Wangedigala Mountain and the Sabaragamuwa Plains, with the rocky outcrop of Bambaragala forming the backdrop as the water plunges past you. It's rated Extreme and is one of CEA's signature descents.

diyaluma-falls.shortDescription: Descend 625 feet of Sri Lanka's second-highest waterfall, with plunge pools at the top for a post-abseil swim.
fullDescription: Diyaluma Falls plunges 220 metres (720 ft) off the Koslanda plateau, making it Sri Lanka's second-highest waterfall, easily reached from Ella or Haputhale. The abseil itself covers 625 feet of the face, with mist and spray for company most of the way down.
At the top, a cluster of natural plunge pools offers a few playful jumps before you begin the descent — a nice reward for the hike in.

laxapana-falls.shortDescription: Rappel down a 415-foot waterfall steeped in local legend, framed by the notorious 'Seven Virgins' peaks.
fullDescription: Laxapana Falls drops 126 metres in Maskeliya, ranked among Sri Lanka's highest waterfalls, and is one of CEA's most popular abseils. Local folklore ties the site to the Buddha himself, and the name — from 'laxa' (a hundred thousand) and 'pahana' (lamp) — nods to the light said to radiate from the falls.
As you descend the 415-foot face, you'll pass in view of the Seven Virgins peaks, site of a well-known plane crash, adding a dramatic backdrop to an already striking descent.

gartmore-falls.shortDescription: Rappel 400 feet down a waterfall tumbling into the Maskeliya reservoir, with an infinity-pool view from the top.
fullDescription: Gartmore Falls drops 400 feet into the Maskeliya reservoir, reached via a scenic drive through tea plantations en route to Adam's Peak. From the summit, an infinity-pool-style viewpoint looks out over the reservoir before the abseil begins.
It's a full rappel down the rock face beside the falling water — mist, noise, and all — finishing with a sense of having properly earned the view.

gerandi-ella-falls.shortDescription: A beginner-friendly 200-foot abseil down one of seven cascades in the Knuckles Range, reached by a moderate hike from Kandy.
fullDescription: Gerandi Ella is a cluster of seven cascading falls in the Knuckles Mountain Range near Kalugala village, with a combined height of 240–250 metres. CEA's abseil covers the topmost drop, around 200 feet (61 m), reached via a roughly 60-km drive from Kandy and a moderately challenging hike.
From the summit, the view takes in Dumbanagala, Yahangala, and Namunukula across the UNESCO-listed Knuckles biosphere reserve.

kotaganga-ella-falls.shortDescription: A chill, beginner-friendly abseil down a 70-foot drop, part of a hundred-metre cascade deep in the Knuckles Range.
fullDescription: Kotaganga Ella Falls is a multi-tiered cascade in the Knuckles Mountain Range with at least seven distinct segments and a combined height over 100 metres. The 6–7 km hike in from Thangappuwa passes through untouched jungle before reaching the topmost fall, where CEA guides a 70-foot abseil down the rock face.
Rated Chill, it's one of the more accessible descents in the Knuckles — a good pick for a first abseil.

rikili-ella-falls.shortDescription: A 330-foot abseil near Bulathkohupitiya that starts easy and finishes with a self-belay over an overhang.
fullDescription: Rikili Ella drops 330 feet near Bulathkohupitiya and is reached by an easy, under-an-hour hike with views of Narangala Mountain and Olu Ella waterfall along the way.

The first 50 metres are a straightforward descent with plenty of spray, before the route steps out over an overhang that has you self-belaying in open air. It's an accessible abseil overall, with just enough of a twist to make it memorable.

lanka-ella.shortDescription: A gentle 100-foot abseil down an untouched waterfall near Bambarakanda, with a plunge pool shaped like Sri Lanka itself.
fullDescription: Tucked in a valley about a kilometre from Bambarakanda Falls, Lanka Ella is a quieter, less-visited cascade reached on foot through mountainous terrain. At roughly 30 metres with a clean, straight rock face, it's one of CEA's easiest abseils — a good starting point for first-timers.
The pool at its base is said to resemble the outline of Sri Lanka, a small detail that adds to the spot's off-the-beaten-path charm.

kithal-ella.shortDescription: A short, easy abseil down a hidden cascade near Ella, reached along a scenic railway track.
fullDescription: Kithal Ella sits just 2.4 km from Ella, accessible only by following the railway line, and is often overshadowed by the more famous Ravana Falls nearby. CEA's abseil here covers 265 feet down the rock face — a manageable, Chill-rated descent well suited to first-timers.
Local legend links the area to the Ramayana's telling of Princess Sita, with some debate over whether this is in fact the 'true' Ravana Ella — an intriguing footnote to a peaceful, easy outing.

sandun-ella-falls.shortDescription: A relaxed, year-round abseil near Kithulgala, with a good chance of spotting purple-faced leaf monkeys and black eagles.
fullDescription: Sandun Ella Falls is a short, 70-foot abseil just 5 km from Kithulgala, reached via a scenic drive through tea estates. It's accessible year-round and rated Chill, making it a solid pick for beginners or anyone short on time.
Keep an eye out along the way for purple-faced leaf monkeys and black eagles, both regulars in this stretch of forest.

dolukanda.shortDescription: A 350-foot rock-face abseil from the summit of a 600-metre monolith steeped in Hanuman folklore.
fullDescription: Dolukanda is a standalone rock formation rising 600 metres above the surrounding plains near Kurunegala. A two-hour hike through jungle leads to the summit, where a 350-foot sheer rock wall sets up the abseil — 360-degree views included.

Local legend credits the Monkey God Hanuman with bringing the rock from the Himalayas, and the summit itself holds hidden rock pools, a cave with local history, and an ancient temple dating back to the 3rd century BC at its base.

kuwenigala.shortDescription: Scramble and rock-climb to the summit of Kuwenigala, then abseil 220 feet back down — beginner-friendly despite the drama.
fullDescription: Kuwenigala is a massive inselberg near Kurunegala, its summit reached by scrambling through dense vegetation and climbing the lower rock faces. Once at the top, the descent is a 220-foot abseil down the same rock.

Despite the full-on rock-climbing approach, it's considered accessible for beginners with CEA's guides and gear. The rock takes its name from Kuweni, a legendary aboriginal woman said to have placed the distinctive boulder at its peak.

govinda-hela.shortDescription: Rappel 615 feet down Sri Lanka's tallest abseil, a rock known locally as 'Westminster Abbey' for its silhouette.
fullDescription: Govinda Hela rises 500 metres above sea level in Sri Lanka's Eastern Province, its ruins tracing back to the reign of King Buwanekabahu. Colonial-era Brits nicknamed it 'Westminster Abbey' for its resemblance to the London landmark.

It now holds the record for Sri Lanka's tallest abseil — a 615-foot descent, the second-tallest in the world. The rocky ascent to the top passes through biodiverse forest, and the summit delivers a 360-degree view over tanks, lakes, and ebony-tree landscapes.

lakegala.shortDescription: A tough, near-vertical scramble up the 'Rock of Lanka', finishing with a short abseil from the summit.
fullDescription: Lakegala's triangular silhouette dominates the eastern end of the Knuckles range, often compared to Europe's Matterhorn. The route starts in the valley near the remote village of Meemure, following streams and pools before the terrain steepens into a near-vertical rock face.
It's a serious undertaking — 10.5 km with over 850 m of elevation gain — that mixes hiking, scrambling, and a short abseil near the top, set within the UNESCO-listed Knuckles biosphere.

sphinx-ii-hike.shortDescription: A tough hike to two rock formations named for their resemblance to the mythical Sphinx, deep in the Knuckles.
fullDescription: Sphinx II refers to a pair of rocks — Kinihirigala-1 and Kinihirigala-2 — near Corbett's Gap in the Knuckles Massif, named for their likeness to the mythological sphinx. The hike in is a tough 8 km with steep slopes and a route that isn't always obvious, set among peaks like Aliyawetunaela Mountain in a UNESCO-listed biodiversity hotspot.
It rewards the effort with genuine seclusion — this isn't one of the more heavily trafficked Knuckles routes.

yahangala.shortDescription: A steep, mythology-steeped scramble to a summit said to be the resting place of the demon king Ravana.
fullDescription: Yahangala — the 'Bed-Rock' southeast of the Knuckles — is about ninety minutes from Kandy and combines jungle hiking with a near-vertical scramble up the final stretch. Local lore holds that Ravana rests here for eternity, and that the Veddah deity Gale Bandara still watches over the rock.
The 6-km route gains 450 m and is rated Tough, though CEA notes it's manageable for motivated beginners. From the summit, the Knuckles panorama takes in the Mahaweli River and the valley below.

manigala.shortDescription: A moderate hike to a secluded Knuckles plateau nicknamed 'Measuring Rock', rewarded with sweeping, mist-draped views.
fullDescription: Manigala is a secluded outcrop deep in the Knuckles massif, known locally as the 'Measuring Rock' for the way its climb tests those who attempt it. The 11-km hike gains 600 m through dense jungle and rugged canyon terrain before opening onto panoramic views of the mist-covered Knuckles range.
Its remoteness keeps visitor numbers low, and the surrounding villages still hold onto traditions that add some cultural texture to the trek.

kanawiddagala.shortDescription: A tough scramble to the summit of a rock said to be the deadliest hike in Sri Lanka — not for beginners.
fullDescription: Kanawiddagala rises sharply from the Knuckles Mountain Range, its narrow, exposed summit dropping away on all sides — a reputation that's earned it a name as one of the country's more demanding hikes. The 8-km route with 600 m of elevation gain is steeped in Ramayana folklore, tied to the tale of King Ravana and Sita.
It's a roughly two-hour ascent that rewards the effort with genuinely dramatic summit views, mist permitting.

kurullangala.shortDescription: A demanding climb to 5,000-year-old cave art on 'Bird Rock', reserved for experienced climbers.
fullDescription: Kurullangala — 'Bird Rock' — sits on the western side of the Ella Gap and is known for ancient cave art near its summit, depicting birds and human figures believed to be over 5,000 years old.

Reaching it means pulling through dense jungle using roots and vines to scale sheer rock and boulders, so this one's reserved for climbers with real upper-body strength and prior experience. Proper footwear and clothing that can handle thick vegetation are essential.

kodi-ara-kanda.shortDescription: A misty hike to 'Flag Rock' in the Piduruthalagala range, past agricultural villages and a solitary flag-marked summit.
fullDescription: Kodi Ara Kanda — 'Flag Rock' — stands in the Piduruthalagala mountain range and is only reached from the misty Mandaram Nuwara valley. The 7-km route follows a stream through lush foothills where locals farm vegetables, climbing steadily into enveloping mist.
At the summit, a lone tree branch strung with flags marks the top, with glimpses of Sri Lanka's tallest mountain visible whenever the clouds part.

katusukonda.shortDescription: A moderate ridge walk above Kandy nicknamed 'Lizard's Spine', with sheer drops on both sides.
fullDescription: Katusukonda is a narrow rocky ridge on the Hanthana Mountain Range just outside Kandy, its Sinhala name translating roughly to 'lizard's spine'. The 5-km route gains 400 m and traces the ridgeline with drops on either side, opening onto views of Kandy, the Mahaweli River, and the valley below.
Best saved for clear, dry weather — the rock gets genuinely slippery when wet.

alagalla.shortDescription: A popular beginner hike through jungle and grassy slopes to a rocky summit known as 'The Lion's Maw'.
fullDescription: The Alagalla range once served as a defensive line against colonial forces, including the historic Battle of Balana, and today is one of the more approachable hikes in CEA's roster.
The 7.6-km route climbs 520 m through jungle before opening onto grassy slopes leading to the summit ridge, 'The Lion's Maw', where the final approach involves a bit of light rock scrambling.

devils-staircase.shortDescription: A two-day trek and camp from Ohiya to the Horton Plains area, descending into a gorge for a beginner abseil.
fullDescription: This two-day, 17-km trek starts at Ohiya Railway Station and follows a pine-lined road toward Horton Plains, passing tea estates and a small village in the West Udaweriya area along the way. Camp is set at Weli Wanguwa ('Sand Bend'), with a bathing spot just 50 metres from the tents.
Day two descends into a gorge to Lanka Ella waterfall for a beginner-friendly abseil, rounding out a route that mixes trekking, camping, and a proper waterfall descent.

bakers-bend.shortDescription: A two-day camping and trekking route through the Belihul Oya highlands, finishing with a multi-height abseil at Nonpareil Falls.
fullDescription: Starting at Belihul Oya, this two-day route crosses the Kari Watta estate and follows the Belihul Oya river canyon through grassy hills and pine forest, climbing to the Baker's Bend viewpoint for sweeping views over the valley.

Camp is set near Nonpareil Falls, with day two given over to abseiling — heights on this route range from 20 to 200 feet across the falls' several drops. At 12 km and 900 m of elevation gain, it's rated Tough, and the cool, temperate climate here means fewer leeches than lower-altitude routes.

mannakethi-ella.shortDescription: A canyoning route through twin waterfalls and a 70-foot abseil, finishing with rock-pool jumps in Kithulgala.
fullDescription: Mannakethi Ella runs along the Girankitha Oya near Kithulgala, opening with an upper section featuring twin falls and a wide basin suited to technical jumps.

The route continues to a lower fall where CEA guides a 70-foot abseil, set within narrow rock passages and open rock 'stadiums' carved by the water. It's a short, 1-km approach hike, making this one of the more accessible canyoning routes on offer.

katarang-oya.shortDescription: A beginner-friendly canyon near Kithulgala with rock pools, short slides, and a hundred-foot drop through the gorge.
fullDescription: Katarang Oya is a Kelani River tributary near Kithulgala, its open canyon carved to a height of around 100 feet and dotted with rock pools and natural water slides.

The approach is under a kilometre, passing the Broadlands Hydro Power Plant en route, and the terrain suits adventurers of any age or experience level. It's rated Chill — a solid entry point into canyoning before tackling something more technical.

nonpareil-falls.shortDescription: An intermediate canyoning route through a chain of falls near Belihul Oya, with abseils ranging up to nearly 200 feet.
fullDescription: Nonpareil Falls, near Belihul Oya, is a chain of cascades with four separate drops suited to abseiling — ranging from around 32 feet up to a substantial 195 feet. It's designed as a step up from beginner canyoning, letting you build technique across a series of increasingly serious descents.
The site sits beside the Baker's Bend viewpoint, and pairs naturally with an overnight camping trip for a fuller two-day adventure in the Horton Plains foothills.

kithulgala-rafting-adventure.shortDescription: A 3.5 km beginner whitewater run through seven rapids on the Kelani River, Sri Lanka's original rafting spot.
fullDescription: Kithulgala sits on the Kelani River's final stretch of navigable rapids, long established as Sri Lanka's classic whitewater destination and the filming location for Bridge on the River Kwai.

This beginner-friendly run covers 3.5 km and seven rapids up to Class III, with a short slide thrown in, all easily reached off the Colombo–Hatton road. Watch for eagles, macaques, and purple-faced leaf monkeys along the forested banks between rapids.

full-day-rafting-kelani-river.shortDescription: A 12 km full-day whitewater run on the Kelani River, from Class III rapids to a relaxed float through the flatwater.
fullDescription: This full-day route covers 12 km of the Kelani River, opening with the same 3.5 km of Class II–III rapids as the beginner run before easing into gentler Class II water for the remainder.

It's built for people who want more time on the water — passing forested banks, mountain views, and small riverside villages along the way. Wildlife spotting is part of the appeal here, with birds and monkeys regular sightings between rapids.

kala-wewa-kayaking.shortDescription: Paddle a 5th-century reservoir built by King Dhatusena, with elephants often visible along the shoreline at dusk.
fullDescription: Kala Wewa is a twin-reservoir complex — Kala Wewa and Balalu Wewa — built around 460 AD under King Dhatusena, with a combined capacity of 123 million cubic metres. Paddling through Kala Wewa National Park, you're tracing the outline of one of the island's oldest surviving feats of hydraulic engineering.

Local legend credits a jungle-dwelling man named Kadawara for guiding the king to the site. Evenings often bring elephants down to the water's edge, with sunset light adding a fitting finish to the paddle.
